items.sentence_raw: The port city provides a fascinating and rich understanding of the movement of people and goods around the world.
We understand a port as a centre of land-sea exchange, and as a major source of livelihood and a major force for cultural mixing.
But do ports all produce a range of common urban characteristics which justify classifying port cities together under a single generic label?
Do they have enough in common to warrant distinguishing them from other kinds of cities?
A port must be distinguished from a harbour.
They are two very different things.
Most ports have poor harbours, and many fine harbours see few ships.
Harbour is a physical concept, a shelter for ships; port is an economic concept, a centre of land-sea exchange which requires good access to a hinterland even more than a sea-linked foreland.
It is landward access, which is productive of goods for export and which demands imports, that is critical.
Poor harbours can be improved with breakwaters and dredging if there is a demand for a port.
Madras and Colombo are examples of harbours expensively improved by enlarging, dredging and building breakwaters.
items.explain: Q31: The passage says *'Madras and Colombo are examples of harbours expensively improved by enlarging, dredging and building breakwaters'* — this is **'considerable harbour development'**. So the answer is **D**.

items.sentence_raw: Port cities become industrial, financial and service centres and political capitals because of their water connections and the urban concentration which arises there and later draws to it railways, highways and air routes.
items.explain: Q40: The passage says port cities grow because of *'water connections'* which later draw *'railways, highways and air routes'* — **'water connections'** include rivers. This supports the idea of **'river connections'**. So the answer is **YES**.

items.sentence_raw: Water transport means cheap access, the chief basis of all port cities.

Many of the world's biggest cities, for example, London, New York, Shanghai, Istanbul, Buenos Aires, Tokyo, Jakarta, Calcutta, Philadelphia and San Francisco began as ports - that is, with land-sea exchange as their major function - but they have since grown disproportionately in other respects so that their port functions are no longer dominant.
items.explain:
Q27: The passage says many big cities *'began as ports'* but later *'their port functions are no longer dominant'* — this means the port is still part of the city's history. The heading **'Once a port city, always a port city'** captures this idea perfectly. So the answer is **ii**.

Q32: The passage lists *'Istanbul, Buenos Aires'* as cities that *'began as ports'* but later *'their port functions are no longer dominant'* — other facilities took over. This matches **'began as ports but other facilities later dominated'**. So the answer is **C**.

items.sentence_raw: They remain different kinds of places from non-port cities and their port functions account for that difference.
Port functions, more than anything else, make a city cosmopolitan.
items.explain: Q28: The passage says port functions *'make a city cosmopolitan'* and that *'races, cultures, and ideas... jostle, mix and enrich each other'* — **'cosmopolitan'** means **'international'**. The heading **'A truly international environment'** matches this exactly. So the answer is **i**.

items.sentence_raw: A port city is open to the world.
In it races, cultures, and ideas, as well as goods from a variety of places, jostle, mix and enrich each other and the life of the city.
items.explain: Q28: The passage says port functions *'make a city cosmopolitan'* and that *'races, cultures, and ideas... jostle, mix and enrich each other'* — **'cosmopolitan'** means **'international'**. The heading **'A truly international environment'** matches this exactly. So the answer is **i**.

items.sentence_raw: The smell of the sea and the harbour, the sound of boat whistles or the moving tides are symbols of their multiple links with a wide world, samples of which are present in microcosm within their own urban areas.
Sea ports have been transformed by the advent of powered vessels, whose size and draught have increased.
items.explain: Q29: The passage explains that *'powered vessels, whose size and draught have increased'* made many ports *'less accessible'* — bigger ships could not enter. This directly gives **'Reasons for the decline of ports'**. So the answer is **v**.

items.sentence_raw: Many formerly important ports have become economically and physically less accessible as a result.
items.explain: Q29: The passage explains that *'powered vessels, whose size and draught have increased'* made many ports *'less accessible'* — bigger ships could not enter. This directly gives **'Reasons for the decline of ports'**. So the answer is **v**.

items.sentence_raw: By-passed by most of their former enriching flow of exchange, they have become cultural and economic backwaters or have acquired the character of museums of the past.
Examples of these are Charleston, Salem, Bristol, Plymouth, Surat, Galle, Melaka, Soochow, and a long list of earlier prominent port cities in Southeast Asia, Africa and Latin America.
items.explain: Q33: The passage gives *'Plymouth and Melaka'* as examples of ports that became *'backwaters'* when large ships *'by-passed'* them — they lost importance. This matches **'lost their prominence when large ships could not be accommodated'**. So the answer is **F**.

items.sentence_raw: Much domestic port trade has not been recorded.
What evidence we have suggests that domestic trade was greater at all periods than external trade.
items.explain:
Q30: The passage states *'domestic trade was greater at all periods than external trade'* and that *'trade outside the city is its basic function'* — it compares **domestic** and **external** trade. The heading **'Relative significance of trade and service industry'** fits this comparison. So the answer is **vi**.

Q36: The passage states *'domestic trade was greater at all periods than external trade'* — **'domestic trade'** means trade within the country. This directly supports the question statement. So the answer is **YES**.

items.sentence_raw: Shanghai, for example, did most of its trade with other Chinese ports and inland cities.
Calcutta traded mainly with other parts of India and so on.
Most of any city's population is engaged in providing goods and services for the city itself.
items.explain: Q37: The passage says *'Most of any city's population is engaged in providing goods and services for the city itself'* — not international trade. The question says most people are in **'international trade and finance'**, which is the opposite. So the answer is **NO**.

The heading **'Relative significance of trade and service industry'** fits this comparison. So the answer is **vi**.

items.sentence_raw: But each basic worker requires food, housing, clothing and other such services.
Estimates of the ratio of basic to service workers range from 1:4 to 1:8.
No city can be simply a port but must be involved in a variety of other activities.
The port function of the city draws to it raw materials and distributes them in many other forms.
items.explain: Q38: The passage explains that ports *'draw to it raw materials'* and lead to *'refining raw materials or turning them into finished goods'* — this attracts many related industries. This supports the idea of **'subsidiary and independent industries'**. So the answer is **YES**.

items.sentence_raw: Ports take advantage of the need for breaking up the bulk material where water and land transport meet and where loading and unloading costs can be minimised by refining raw materials or turning them into finished goods.
items.explain: Q38: The passage explains that ports *'draw to it raw materials'* and lead to *'refining raw materials or turning them into finished goods'* — this attracts many related industries. This supports the idea of **'subsidiary and independent industries'**. So the answer is **YES**.

items.sentence_raw: The major examples here are oil refining and ore refining, which are commonly located at ports.
It is not easy to draw a line around what is and is not a port function.
All ports handle, unload, sort, alter, process, repack, and reship most of what they receive.
A city may still be regarded as a port city when it becomes involved in a great range of functions not immediately involved with ships or docks.
items.explain: Q35: The passage directly says *'A city may still be regarded as a port city when it becomes involved in a great range of functions not immediately involved with ships or docks'* — this contradicts the question. The question says cities **'cease'** to be port cities, but the passage says they **'may still be regarded'** as such. So the answer is **NO**.

items.sentence_raw: Cities which began as ports retain the chief commercial and administrative centre of the city close to the waterfront.
The centre of New York is in lower Manhattan between two river mouths, the City of London is on the Thames, Shanghai along the Bund.

This proximity to water is also true of Boston, Philadelphia, Bombay, Calcutta, Madras, Singapore, Bangkok, Hong Kong and Yokohama, where the commercial, financial, and administrative centres are still grouped around their harbours even though each city has expanded into a metropolis.
items.explain: Q34: The passage says *'Singapore, Bangkok, Hong Kong and Yokohama'* still have their centres *'grouped around their harbours'* — the business centre stays near the water. This matches **'maintain their business centres near the port waterfront'**. So the answer is **G**.

items.sentence_raw: Even a casual visitor cannot mistake them as anything but port cities.
